about.label: About the park
about.heading: An urban oasis by the Mekong
about.lead: Located in the center of Vientiane, Chao Anouvong Park stretches along the Mekong River and is one of the city's most popular public spaces.
about.paragraph1: The park is named after King Anouvong, a famous figure in Lao history. His bronze statue stands tall, holding a sword in one hand and pointing towards Thailand across the Mekong with the other, symbolizing the independence and dignity of the Lao people.
about.paragraph2: During the day, it is a lush green promenade; in the evening, as the Mekong sunset turns the sky golden, the park transforms into a vibrant night market and a hub for citizen recreation.
about.quote: Here you can see the most authentic street life of Vientiane and the most beautiful sunset.

history.label: History & Legends
history.heading: The Gaze of King Chao Anouvong
history.intro: The park's name and its central statue carry the Lao people's deep memory of independence and dignity.

timeline.title: Birth of a king
timeline.text: Chao Anouvong is born in the Kingdom of Vientiane — the last crown prince who would later become its final king.

timeline.title: The uprising against Siam
timeline.text: He leads a revolt to reclaim Lao independence. Vientiane is devastated in the war, yet his defiance turns him into a national hero.

timeline.title: Park & bronze statue unveiled
timeline.text: Completed for the 450th anniversary of Vientiane's founding: a bronze statue of the king — about 14 metres tall including its base — rises on the Mekong shore.

timeline.title: Heart of the riverside city
timeline.text: A symbol of Vientiane and the living centre of riverside civic life — where history and daily life meet.

narrative.subtitle: The hero-king who gazes at the great river
narrative.text: At the centre of the park stands the bronze statue of King Chao Anouvong, about 8 metres tall (about 14 metres including its base). In armour, his right hand grips a sword while his left hand points firmly across the Mekong toward Thailand. Chao Anouvong (1767–1829) was the last ruler of the Vientiane Kingdom and a symbol of Lao independence and dignity.

narrative.subtitle: The final echo of 1826
narrative.text: In the early 19th century, Laos was under Siamese (Thai) control. In 1826, King Chao Anouvong launched a struggle for national independence. Though the uprising failed against overwhelming odds and the old city of Vientiane was destroyed, his spirit of defending his homeland's honour made him an eternal hero in the Lao people's hearts.

narrative.subtitle: The naga and the guardian of the river
narrative.text: In Lao belief, the Mekong is not only a life-giving mother river but also the home of the Phaya Naga — a mythical dragon. Local legend holds that the king's statue stands guard on the bank alongside the naga, blessing Vientiane with peace and prosperity. On traditional festivals such as Boun Lai Heua Fai (the end-of-lent river festival), tens of thousands of citizens gather along the park's riverfront to float thousands of flower lanterns, carrying reverence for history and wishes for the future.

statue.title: The king's gaze and gesture
statue.text: One hand rests a sword at his side; the other reaches toward the opposite bank (Nong Khai, Thailand). In local lore this gesture is both a declaration of Laos's former territory and dignity, and a blessing upon those who come after.

naga.title: The Mekong dragon (Phaya Naga)
naga.text: Lao folklore is intertwined with the naga of the Mekong. Locals believe a dragon dwells at the riverbed beneath the park, protecting the land. Each year during Boun Lai Heua Fai, citizens float lanterns and hold boat races by the river to honour the river spirit and the naga.

champa.title: The Champa flower (Dok Champa)
champa.text: Beyond the frangipani in the garden, the Dok Champa — Laos's national flower — symbolises purity, devotion and the gentle hospitality of the Lao people. Offerings of marigold or champa garlands at the statue's base are a quiet way to pay respect.

legend.title: Memory of a national hero
legend.text: In Lao historical narrative, Chao Anouvong is synonymous with courage. Locals often lay flowers and incense before the statue to express respect and remembrance.

didYouKnow.title: Did you know?
didYouKnow.text: This is one of the largest bronze statues in Laos. On special occasions the base is surrounded by flowers during grand commemorations.

folklore.title: Life by the river
folklore.tale: For Vientiane residents, the Mekong is both a natural border and the centre of life. Evening river breezes carry away the day's heat as people gather, continuing a riverside way of life passed down through generations.
folklore.shrine: Near the king's statue, please keep an appropriate reverence — no disrespectful gestures or climbing the base.

concrete.title: Modern landscape, historic depth
concrete.text: The park's design balances modern urban planning with historical commemoration. Open plazas, tidy paths and the stately statue together give Vientiane's centre a rare sense of openness.

sisterQuote.title: A conversation across one river
sisterQuote.text: Standing in the park, across the broad Mekong lies Thailand's Nong Khai province. At night, the lights of both banks mirror each other, telling of the ancient civilisation nurtured by this great river.

items.title: ✈️ Airport to the park (Wattay Intl. VTE)
items.desc: Wattay International Airport is about 3–5 km away, roughly 15–25 min by car. Step-by-step:
steps: After baggage claim, exit the arrivals hall and look for the bright-yellow LOCA / InDrive taxi point outside the terminal, or connect to airport Wi-Fi and book via the app.
In the app, or tell the driver the destination: Chao Anouvong Park (riverside, Mekong).
Alternatively, buy a fixed-fare ticket at the taxi counter in the arrivals hall — about 150,000 Kip, assigned to a licensed taxi.
The car goes via Route 13 or the city centre to Fa Ngum Road; get off at the park entrance and walk straight to the statue and riverside promenade.
Fare guide: app ride about 60,000–120,000 Kip; avoid unmetered tuk-tuks to prevent overcharging. After 17:30 the riverside gets congested, so allow extra time.

faqs.a: The park is a fully open public green space with no ticket — free and open 24 hours a day.

faqs.q: How long should I plan to visit?
faqs.a: Allow 1.5–3 hours: ~30 min at the statue and riverside walk, ~30 min watching the Mekong sunset from the steps, and 1–2 hours at the night market for food and crafts.

faqs.q: Are there toilets or luggage storage?
faqs.a: Public toilets are available in the park and around the night market, costing about 2,000–3,000 Lao kip (bring small change and tissues). There is no luggage storage inside the park — leave large bags at your hotel or use a nearby café's service.

faqs.q: How do I get to the park?
faqs.a: It sits on the Mekong in central Vientiane. Walk 10–15 min from the city centre; use the LOCA or InDrive apps (set destination to Chao Anouvong Park); or take a tuk-tuk and show the driver 'Night Market' / 'Chao Anouvong Statue'.

faqs.q: Can I drive and park nearby?
faqs.a: After 17:30 the riverside Fa Ngum Road gets very congested — four-wheel parking is not advised. Bikes/motorbikes can use marked roadside bays (a small fee of about 5,000 kip may apply).

faqs.q: What payment is accepted at the night market?
faqs.a: Most stalls are cash only. Carry Lao kip (LAK); some accept Thai baht (THB) or US dollars but change is given in kip at a loss. Local apps like BCEL One work at a few shops, but cards are rarely usable at stalls.
The night market is generally clean. If you have a sensitive stomach: choose hot, freshly grilled or boiled items; be cautious with raw seafood or cut fruit; ask for 'no ice' in drinks.

faqs.q: How should I behave at the statue?
faqs.a: The king is a sacred national hero. Dress modestly (no beachwear), never climb the base or railing, and avoid playful or disrespectful gestures. You may lay marigold or champa garlands at the offering altar.

Not recommended without permission. The park borders the Mekong international boundary (Thailand opposite) and lies near government and diplomatic areas — an unauthorised drone risks confiscation or a heavy fine.

faqs.q: Is the park safe at night?
faqs.a: Very safe. Vientiane is peaceful and the park is well lit, with many local families around. Still, watch your bag, phone and wallet in crowds.
From Feb to Apr (late dry season) agricultural burning can raise the AQI and haze the sky, so sunsets may glow red rather than golden. Consider a mask if you are sensitive.

faqs.q: What are the opening hours of Chao Anouvong Park?
faqs.a: The park is an open riverside green space with no gates, so it is accessible 24 hours a day, every day. The night market along Fa Ngum Road usually runs from about 18:00 to 22:30.

faqs.q: What time does the Vientiane night market open?
faqs.a: Stalls begin setting up around 17:30–18:00 and wind down by roughly 22:30, every evening. Food, clothes and souvenirs line the promenade beside the park.

faqs.q: What is the Chao Anouvong statue?
faqs.a: A bronze monument of King Anouvong (r. 1805–1828), about 8 metres tall (about 14 metres including its base), unveiled in 2010, facing across the Mekong toward Thailand. It honours the last king of Vientiane and is the park's centrepiece.

faqs.q: What is near Chao Anouvong Park?
faqs.a: It sits on Vientiane's central riverfront. A short walk away: the night market, the Fa Ngum promenade, Patuxai (Victory Monument) and Wat Si Saket.

facilities.label: Services & facilities
facilities.heading: Visitor Services & Nearby Facilities
facilities.lead: Practical amenities around the park, listed by type so you can plan ahead. We recommend by category only and are not affiliated with any vendor.
facilities.note: Facility types available near the park; specific venues change, so confirm on arrival.

categories.name: Public restrooms
categories.desc: Public toilets sit near the promenade and the night-market entrance, generally free or for a small upkeep fee. Bring small change and tissues.

categories.name: Parking
categories.desc: Street parking lines the riverside Fa Ngum Road. During the evening peak (after 17:30) it fills fast; paid lots and roadside bays appear nearby, and two-wheelers have marked bays.

categories.name: Dining & cafés
categories.desc: Riverside restaurants, coffee shops and the night-market food stalls ring the park. Choose busy, well-lit stalls for the freshest food.

categories.name: Lodging
categories.desc: Hotels, guesthouses and hostels sit within a short walk or tuk-tuk ride in the city centre — handy if you want the sunrise or late-night market.

categories.name: Shops & convenience
categories.desc: Convenience stores, ATMs and small shops cluster in the surrounding blocks for water, snacks and essentials.

categories.name: Fuel & EV charging
categories.desc: Petrol stations and EV charging points are found along the main avenues in the city, not inside the park — top up before you arrive by car.

categories.name: Accessibility
categories.desc: The riverside promenade is flat and paved with ramps and frequent benches; the open plaza around the statue is step-free.

categories.name: Lighting & safety
categories.desc: The park and riverfront are well lit at night with a steady local presence; keep bags close in crowds.

transport.label: Getting there
transport.heading: How to Get to Chao Anouvong Park
transport.lead: The park sits on the Mekong in central Vientiane. Here are the practical ways in, from the airport to your own two feet.
transport.tip: Set the destination to “Chao Anouvong Park” or “Mekong Night Market” in any map app — both drop you at the riverside.

modes.name: From Wattay Airport (VTE)
modes.desc: Wattay International is about 3–5 km west, roughly 15–25 minutes by road.
steps: After baggage claim, use the airport Wi-Fi and book a licensed taxi or ride via the LOCA / InDrive apps, or buy a fixed-fare ticket at the arrivals taxi counter (around 100,000–150,000 LAK).
Set the destination to Chao Anouvong Park (riverside, Mekong); the car runs via Route 13 and Fa Ngum Road to the park entrance.
After ~17:30 the riverside gets congested, so allow extra time and meet your driver at the agreed pickup point.

modes.name: Public transit & city bus
modes.desc: Vientiane's city buses and shared songthaews run along the avenues near the riverfront.
steps: Find a bus or songthaew heading toward the riverfront / city centre and alight near Fa Ngum Road.
From the stop it is a short walk to the statue and the promenade.
Keep small change ready; fares are low but conductors may not give change for large notes.

modes.name: Taxi & ride-hailing
modes.desc: Metered taxis and app rides (LOCA, InDrive) are the easiest door-to-door option.
steps: Book in the app or ask your hotel to call a metered taxi; show the driver “Chao Anouvong Park / Night Market”.
From most central hotels it is about 5–10 minutes to the riverside.
Agree a price first for street taxis without a meter to avoid surprises.

modes.name: Tuk-tuk & songthaew
modes.desc: Three-wheel tuk-tuks and shared songthaews are everywhere and happy to negotiate.
steps: Tell the driver “Night Market” or “Chao Anouvong Statue” and agree a fare before boarding.
They can drop you right at the promenade entrance off Fa Ngum Road.

modes.name: Bicycle
modes.desc: Flat, bike-friendly terrain and a riverside path make cycling pleasant, especially at dawn and dusk.
steps: Rent a bicycle from a city guesthouse or shop, then follow the riverfront path east to the park.
Use the marked roadside bays for parking; a small fee may apply.

modes.name: On foot from the city centre
modes.desc: Most riverside landmarks are within a 15–30 minute walk.
steps: From Patuxai, Wat Si Saket or the morning market, walk toward the Mekong and follow the river north/south to the statue.
It is a flat, shaded walk — a nice way to arrive before sunset.

responsibility.label: Respect & protect
responsibility.heading: Science & Visitor Responsibility
responsibility.lead: A few facts and habits that keep the park, the Mekong and its wildlife healthy for everyone.
responsibility.river: The Mekong is a working, flowing river — not a swimming pool. Currents and boats make swimming unsafe, and the water quality varies with the season and upstream activity. Enjoy it from the promenade and never litter into it.
wildlife: River birds and egrets feeding at the water's edge at dawn and dusk.
The occasional monitor lizard or otter along the banks — watch quietly, never feed.
Dok Champa and frangipani filling the gardens with scent.
zeroWaste: Use the bins for night-market packaging and bring a reusable bottle.
Keep the king's statue and riverfront clean and respectful.
safety: Carry water and use sunscreen in the hot dry season (Feb–Apr).
After rain, paths can be slippery — wear sensible shoes.
Watch your bag and phone in night-market crowds.
responsibility.culture: Chao Anouvong is a revered national hero. Dress modestly near the statue, never climb the base or railing, and you may lay a champa or marigold garland at the offering altar.
